book.unit_title: Major geological processes associated with plate tectonics

title: External (exogenic) forces
competency: Explain weathering, erosion and deposition by water, wind and the sea, and mass wasting, with their landforms.

keywords.def: The breaking down of rocks in place, physically or chemically.
The lowering of the land by weathering and erosion.
The removal and movement of soil and rock particles by water, wind, waves or ice.
Downslope movement of rock, regolith and soil under gravity.

en.text: Weathering breaks rocks down where they lie. Physical weathering makes smaller pieces of the same rock: exfoliation from daily heating and cooling in hot deserts, frost action that leaves screes, and roots and burrowing animals. Chemical weathering changes the minerals: rain with oxygen rusts iron, rain with carbonic acid dissolves limestone into caves with stalactites and stalagmites, as at Sof Omar, and bacteria and organic acids break minerals down.

screens.title: Peeling rocks
screens.ask: In a hot desert, rocks heat up by day and cool at night. Over years their outer layers
opts: turn into sand dunes at once
screens.after: Repeated expansion and contraction makes the surface layers peel off: exfoliation.

screens.title: Physical weathering
paras: Rocks break into pieces with the same chemistry.
Thermal expansion and contraction → exfoliation (hot, dry areas).
Frost action: water freezes and expands in cracks; fragments pile up as screes.
Plant roots widen cracks; worms, moles and rabbits break rock as they dig.

screens.title: Chemical weathering
paras: The minerals themselves change.
Rainwater carries O₂ and CO₂: iron rusts; carbonic acid dissolves limestone (solution or carbonation); hydrolysis makes clay.
Limestone caves form, e.g. Sof Omar on the Weyb river in Bale.
Stalactites hang from the ceiling; stalagmites grow from the floor; joined, they make pillars.
Bacteria and organic acids from decaying plants also break minerals down.

en.text: Running water is the most powerful external agent; its power grows with speed and slope and falls where vegetation is thick. Runoff causes sheet, rill and gully erosion. In its upper course a river cuts V-shaped valleys, gorges, interlocking spurs, rapids and waterfalls; in the middle course it meanders and forms ox-bow lakes; in the lower course it deposits flood plains and deltas.

screens.after: Vegetation slows the water and holds the soil; bare slopes in the highlands quickly form gullies.

Faster water on steeper slopes erodes more; vegetation protects.
Sheet erosion: thin even layer of topsoil removed.
Rill erosion: small channels.
Gully erosion: rills join and cut deep, wide gullies.

en.text: In deserts and semi-deserts wind builds sand dunes around obstacles, crescent-shaped barchans, and carries fine dust (loess) beyond the deserts, as in North China. Sea waves erode and deposit along coasts, forming beaches, spits (narrow sand ridges attached at one end) and lagoons (salt water cut off by sand banks).

paras: Strongest in deserts and semi-deserts.
Sand dunes: hills of sand that collect around obstacles.

Loess: fertile fine dust laid down by wind, e.g. North China.

screens.title: The work of the sea
paras: Waves erode and deposit along coasts.
Beach: a strip of coast covered with sediment.
Spit: a narrow sand or silt ridge joined to land at one end.
Lagoon: salt water separated from the sea by sand banks.

en.text: Mass wasting is the downslope movement of rock, regolith and soil under gravity. Water helps by filling pores and reducing cohesion; slopes steeper than about 25–40° become unstable; and people make it worse through farming and overgrazing on steep slopes. Landslides have destroyed lives and property in parts of Ethiopia.

screens.title: Rainy season slopes
screens.ask: Why are landslides on Ethiopian hillsides most common in the rainy season?
opts: Soaked soil loses cohesion and slides under gravity
screens.after: Water fills the spaces between particles and weakens the slope.

screens.title: Causes of mass wasting
paras: Gravity is the controlling force.
Water: soaks in, fills pores, reduces cohesion between particles.
Slope angle: materials stay firm only up to about 25–40°; large angular particles hold the steepest slopes.
People: farming and overgrazing on steep, unstable slopes.

screens.title: Key word
defs: Downslope movement of rock, regolith and soil under gravity.
